notes.meaning: Leaders from the clan of Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh came to speak with Moses and the heads of Israel. Earlier, God had granted land to the five daughters of Zelophehad because their father died without leaving any sons. The clan leaders realized that this decision created an unforeseen problem that needed to be settled before Israel entered Canaan.

The leaders reminded Moses of two previous commands from God. First, the Lord had ordered the land of Canaan to be divided by lot among the tribes, and second, He directed Moses to give Zelophehad's share to his daughters. The leaders were not arguing with God's ruling, but showing faith that Israel would truly possess the land.

The leaders explained what would happen if these daughters married men from other Israelite tribes. In their culture, children belonged to their father's tribe, so any inherited land would pass to the husband's clan. This meant the tribe of Manasseh would permanently lose part of the land God had assigned to them.

The Year of Jubilee was a celebration every fifty years when sold property was returned to its original owners. However, the Jubilee only returned land that had been sold, not land passed down through marriage. If these women married outside their tribe, the Jubilee would actually lock the land permanently into the other tribe's possession.

Moses sought the Lord and then answered the people with God's authority. The Lord declared that the leaders of Manasseh were speaking the truth and that their concern was right. God showed that He listens to honest questions and cares about fairness for His people.

God gave a specific command regarding the daughters of Zelophehad. They were given the freedom to choose their own husbands, but they had to marry within a clan of their father's tribe. This rule respected the women's choice while still protecting their tribe's land.

God set down a lasting principle that land in Israel must never be transferred from one tribe to another. Every Israelite was required to hold fast to the property assigned to their ancestral tribe. This protected the divine boundaries God had set so that no tribe would lose its inheritance.

The ruling for Zelophehad's daughters was turned into a general law for all of Israel. Any woman who inherited family land because she had no brothers had to marry within her father's tribe. Women who did not inherit land were still free to marry men from any tribe in Israel.

The Lord repeated the command that no inherited land could ever pass between tribes. Each tribe of Israel was required to preserve its own territory intact. God values order and faithfulness, ensuring that every family and clan kept what He had promised them.

Zelophehad's daughters acted in direct obedience to what the Lord commanded through Moses. They did not push for unlimited freedom, but willingly followed God's boundaries. Their prompt obedience is an encouraging example of trusting God's wisdom.

The five daughters—Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah—married their first cousins on their father's side. In ancient Hebrew culture, marrying a cousin was a common and accepted practice. By doing this, they honored their family line and kept their father's name alive.

The women married within the clans of Manasseh, so their land stayed safely inside their father's tribe. The clan's problem was completely resolved without taking away the property that had been given to the daughters. God's solution brought peace by balancing individual rights with the good of the whole community.

The book of Numbers ends with a summary of the laws the Lord gave through Moses on the plains of Moab, just across the river from Jericho. Israel had traveled through forty years of desert wandering and was now camped at the edge of the Promised Land. God had prepared His people with all the laws and guidance they needed to begin life in Canaan.
